title: Measuring Vision in a Restless Child

patient.name: Ethan Goh
patient.presenting_complaint: Referred by school health service — possible myopia, difficulty seeing the board in class

history.hpc: Ethan is a 7-year-old brought by his mother after his school vision screening flagged reduced distance vision. His mother says he has been squinting at the TV and moving closer to see better. This is his first visit to an eye clinic. Ethan is shy and initially refuses to cooperate — he turns his head away and says 'I don't want to do the eye test.' His mother is present and supportive.
history.pmhx: No known medical conditions. No previous spectacles. No eye surgery. No known allergies.
history.family_hx: Both parents are myopic. Father wears -4.00D glasses.
history.social_hx: Studying in Primary 1. Lives with parents. Watches TV and iPad approximately 3-4 hours daily.

va.right: 6/19 (LogMAR 0.5) — achieved after gentle encouragement, with occluder

iop.right: Not tested — not indicated at this visit

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Not assessed at this stage — PSA role is VA measurement only
examination_findings.fundus: Not assessed — doctor to review after VA obtained

logmar_va.method: LogMAR tumbling-E chart on the M&S Smart system, calibrated to room length, with child-friendly encouragement

diagnosis: VA measurement completed for both eyes. RE 6/19, LE 6/12 unaided — reduced vision in both eyes, right worse than left. Results to be reviewed by doctor. Consistent with early-onset myopia given family history and symptoms.

immediate: Introduce yourself to the child and parent — use the child's name and get down to his level
Explain the test simply: 'I am going to show you some letters, and you just need to point which way the E is facing. Like this!' — demonstrate with your hand
Use the tumbling-E or picture chart (Lea Symbols) for children who cannot name letters — confirm which chart is appropriate for Ethan's reading ability
Let Ethan hold the occluder rather than placing it on his face — reduces fear and gives him control
Test the right eye first by convention, occluding the left — the same order as for adults
Start from the top (largest) line and work down — the child must get all 5 optotypes on a line before moving to the next, and you stop at the line where he cannot
Be patient and praise the child: 'Well done! That was really good!' between lines
If child cannot cooperate, take a break and try again — do not force
Record results for both eyes separately on the clinic form: unaided VA RE and LE
follow_up: Hand the completed VA form to the nurse or doctor
Inform parent briefly: 'We have completed the vision test — the doctor will review the results and discuss what it means'
Do not tell parents a diagnosis or interpretation of the results
patient_education: Reassure Ethan that he did well and the test is finished
Tell the parent that the doctor will explain the results
If parent asks about glasses, advise her to ask the doctor

key_points: Identifies the patient correctly (confirm name and date of birth with parent)
Notes the child's level of cooperation before starting
Checks if child can recognise letters or needs a picture/tumbling-E chart
Introduces self and explains the test in age-appropriate language
Uses the calibrated room distance shown on the M&S Smart system
Tests each eye separately with the other eye properly occluded
Uses child-appropriate strategies: tests better eye first, lets child hold occluder, uses praise
Records unaided VA for both eyes in LogMAR notation
Recognises result is reduced for a 7-year-old (normal should be 6/6 or better by this age)
Does not interpret or diagnose — correctly defers to doctor
Understands that family history of myopia is a relevant background detail
Identifies the need to re-test if cooperation was inadequate
Uses a child-friendly approach throughout — patience, simple language, praise
Does not force the child — takes a break if cooperation fails
Accurately records results and hands form to clinical staff
Does not give parents any diagnostic information — defers to doctor
